I liked the instructor fine — lectures were clear, and he was obviously trying to make OS ideas approachable — but the rubric on the projects never felt concrete enough for me to know where I was losing points, and feedback came back so late that by the time I understood what I’d done wrong, we were already deep into the next thing. That hurt more than it normally would have because the course is project-heavy and the exams matter a lot, so if you get off track early it kind of lingers. I came in with pretty strong coding experience and not much theory, which honestly is probably why some weeks felt weirdly split for me. The implementation-heavy parts were mostly doable if I stayed on top of them, but the kernel concepts took me longer than I expected to really click. I was also taking a couple other demanding classes at the same time, though the week-to-week time pressure here was usually manageable until exam periods. One thing I didn’t love was that there wasn’t much useful interaction with other students. Maybe that was partly the format, maybe just bad luck with who I ended up around, but it felt like everyone disappeared into their own work and surfaced only when they were stressed. I remember one project week where I spent more time trying to figure out whether I was overengineering a synchronization piece than actually getting help from anyone. That said, I don’t think the course itself is badly designed. For an introductory service course, it does build pretty naturally on the stated prerequisites. I struggled for most of the term and barely passed, but it never felt like I was missing some hidden background class. It was more that the evaluation side of the course made it hard to recover once I stumbled. I’d still recommend it pretty broadly, especially if you want a real introduction to operating systems and you’re okay with learning some lessons the hard way.
